short: A double envelopment that destroyed a Saxon army twice its size in about two hours.
full:
Charles XII was wintering in eastern Poland when a Saxon and Russian army under Johann Matthias von der Schulenburg moved west to cut him off from Sweden. Carl Gustav Rehnskiöld intercepted it near Fraustadt in Silesia on 13 February 1706 with around 9,000 men and no artillery at all, against roughly 20,000 with thirty guns.

Rehnskiöld sent his cavalry round both flanks while the infantry advanced with pike and sword without stopping to trade volleys. Both allied wings folded inward, the centre was surrounded, and the fighting was effectively over within two hours. Saxon losses were about 7,000 dead and 7,000 captured; Swedish dead numbered a few hundred. Several thousand Russian infantry in Saxon service were killed after surrendering, an episode contemporary Swedish accounts pass over in silence. The date given is Gregorian; Sweden's divergent calendar of 1700-1712 made it 3 February. Sabaton's "Killing Ground" takes the battle as its subject.
